scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tinya palla is a traditional dance of Inca origin centered in the Pomabamba Province of the Ancash Region in Peru.
The term derives from Quechua words: 'tinya' (a traditional drum), 'palla' (a lady or noble woman of Inca lineage), and 'wiqru' (meaning twisted or bent).
According to regional tradition, the dance recalls the story of Conchucano princesses who traveled north looking for soldiers sent to fight off invaders.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tinya palla is performed during cultural festivals and community events in Pomabamba.
The dance honors Inca nobility and acts out the mythic journey and loss of the Conchucano warriors who failed to return from battle due to moral corruption.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women wear the pintaybata featuring a dark pollera skirt, a pink monillo blouse, a multi-turn rosary, a short blue or light-blue lliclla shawl, brown leather boots, and a white wool hat with a red ribbon.
They carry a decorated staff called a kiyaya or chuncho.

The yunca character wears a black vest, a white long-sleeved shirt, black trousers secured with a multi-colored sash (faja), sandals, a wool hat adorned with two large feather plumes, and carries a small whip or rein called a culebrilla.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The characters within the dance representation include the gurikuq, the capitana, the six pallas (Inca princesses), and the yunca.
The dance is specific to the Pomabamba Province in the Ancash Region of Peru, occasionally referred to locally as wiqru palla or wicro palla.
Rooted in pre-Columbian Inca traditions and regional mythology of the Conchucos zone, Tinya palla persists as an active heritage tradition in Ancash, Peru.
